YouTube title seed: What Happens to a Railroad Gate When the Power Goes Out?
YouTube description seed: Power cut at a railroad crossing: does the gate stay up or come down? Guess before you watch. Sources: US FHWA Highway-Rail Crossing Handbook; FRA Grade Crossing Toolkit. #TellMeWhyyyyyy #Shorts
The central fact: Crossing gates are built so that power holds them up, and losing power lets gravity bring them down.
The later surprise: Exit gates on some crossings do the opposite and fail up so no car is trapped.
The very first frame shows a red-and-white railroad crossing arm standing raised beside a road, its red lights just starting to flash, the arm visibly twitching as power cuts; the arm does not drop in the first second. Already moving in the first frame; do not reveal the mechanism in the opening.
What changes inside each 6s clip:
Scene 1 (contradiction, 0-6s): Opening: the arm is raised and the red lights start flashing in the first second. About 2s in, the lights flicker and cut out as power fails. About 4s in, the raised arm starts dropping by itself.
Scene 2 (clue, 6-12s): Mechanism starts about 5s in. A real gate mechanism with its housing open, shown as an exposed component (no animation or cutaway); about 2s in, framing moves to the real steel counterweights on the field side; about 4s in, a physical tabletop balance prop with the arm side slightly heavier tips down under a hand.
Scene 3 (mechanism, 12-18s): The raised arm with the power indicator going off; about 2s in, the arm starts lowering smoothly by its own weight; about 4s in, a low angle as it reaches level.
Scene 4 (second_reveal, 18-24s): A four-gate crossing from above; about 2s in, the entry arms are down; about 4s in, the exit arms rise so the lane out stays open.
Scene 5 (payoff, 24-30s): Side view of the lowered gate; about 3s in, return to the exact opening: the same raised arm beside the same road with its lights just starting to flash, same framing as scene 1's first frame, so it loops.
Fact boundaries: US standards only. Exit gates fail up, not down; do not say every gate drops. Mechanism details vary by design; do not claim every gate uses the same motor or brake. No staged incidents or filming at an active crossing; no fake accident.

facts.statement: In the US, the entry gates at railroad crossings are built to fail safe in the down position: power holds them up, and if the power fails they lower by gravity.
Heavy counterweights balance the gate arm, and when the power is lost the mechanism lowers the arm smoothly all the way from straight up to level.
At crossings with exit gates, those exit gates fail safe in the up position so cars are not trapped on the tracks.
